surface_mechanism_description: The ZnO core was etched under electron-beam irradiation, leading to the formation of nanotubes. The etching process was influenced by the presence of defects in the ZnO nanowires and the Al2O3 shell, which facilitated the decomposition of ZnO into Zn and O2, allowing for the formation of nanotubes.
evidence: The presence of abundant internal defects in the ZnO nanowires might induce a weakening of bonding between the compositional elements, thus less energy would be required for chemical bond distortion/breaking in defect-enriched locations via a displacement or sputtering damage process under electron-beam irradiation. However, in the absence of an Al2O3 shell, some vacancies as well as irradiation-induced stress buildup could be self expelled from the nanowires through a relaxation process. Oxygen vacancies could even be eliminated by incorporation of oxygen from the trace oxygen in the TEM chamber. Therefore, irradiation-induced defects would attain thermal equilibrium with a uniform distribution in ZnO, and no obvious damage would occur to the bare ZnO nanowires under beam irradiation during a time-limited observation, as seen in Figure 4. However, with the conformal Al2O3 coating, the rearrangement of irradiation-induced defects at the surface of the ZnO nanowire is blocked. Defects would gather preferentially at the interface between the core and the shell and further develop into voids with continuing beam exposure, and Zn2+ and O2 produced under beam irradiation may more easily diffuse through the amorphous alumina shell than directly vanish into the vacuum of the TEM chamber. Alternatively, the ZnO core could possibly be decomposed in the interfacial voids to yield Zn and O2 vapor under electron-beam irradiation. Most of these species are able to be desorbed by further diffusing out of the Al2O3 shell, while some of them may recrystallize and form ZnO nanocrystals scattered in the shell.
